title: Meeting a new classmate
context: It is your first day in a new class. A classmate says hello.

a.speaker: Sam
a.say: Hi! I am Sam. What is your name?

choices.text: Hi, Sam. I am Amina. Nice to meet you.
choices.feedback: Friendly and complete.
Correct, but add a greeting to sound friendly.

choices.text: Why do you want to know?
choices.feedback: This sounds unfriendly when someone says hello.

b.speaker: Sam
b.say: Nice to meet you, Amina. Where are you from?

choices.text: I am from Somalia. And you?
choices.feedback: Good answer, and you asked a question back.
Correct. A full sentence is better.
Try to say where you are from.

b2.speaker: Sam
b2.say: Oh, sorry. I only wanted to say hello.

choices.text: That is OK. I am Amina. Nice to meet you.
choices.feedback: A kind way to fix the moment.
A short sound does not help the conversation.

title: Ordering a drink at a café
context: You are at a café and want a tea.

choices.feedback: Polite and clear.
Understood, but add "please".
This is too direct and not polite.
Short and polite.
Fine. Add "please".
This does not answer the question.

b2.speaker: Waiter
b2.say: Sorry? Could you ask again, please?

choices.feedback: A good, polite repair.
This ends the conversation badly.
Natural when you pay.
Acceptable, but add thanks.
Rude when the price is fair.

title: Disagreeing with a senior colleague
context: A senior director proposes cutting the training budget. You believe this is a mistake and need to say so without damaging the relationship.

a.speaker: Director
a.say: I think we should cut the training budget entirely this year. It is the easiest saving available.

choices.text: I appreciate the pressure on costs, and I wonder whether we might look at the longer-term picture before we decide.
choices.feedback: Acknowledges the concern, then reframes diplomatically.
Blunt disagreement with a senior colleague closes the discussion.

choices.text: If that is what you think best, I will go along with it.
choices.feedback: Avoids conflict but gives up your point.

b1.speaker: Director
b1.say: Go on. What are you worried about?

choices.text: Our attrition figures suggest that untrained staff leave sooner, so the saving may prove false economy. Might a reduced programme be a fair compromise?
choices.feedback: Evidence plus a constructive alternative.
A vague appeal is easy to dismiss.

choices.text: I simply feel uneasy about it.
choices.feedback: Honest but lacks substance.

b2.speaker: Director
b2.say: I beg your pardon? I would like to hear your reasoning, if you have any.

choices.text: That came across more sharply than I intended. My concern is that the savings may be short-lived, and I would like to explain why.
choices.feedback: A gracious recovery that keeps your argument alive.
Escalates the conflict.

b3.speaker: Director
b3.say: Good. I am glad we are aligned.

choices.text: Actually, before we finalise, could I raise one reservation?
choices.feedback: Reopens the issue politely at the right moment.
You have conceded without voicing a real concern.

e1.speaker: Director
e1.say: That is a fair point. Let us draft a reduced programme and review it next month.

e2.speaker: Director
e2.say: I will think about it, but my inclination stands.
